Tame
tām
v.t. and adj. (to subdue or domesticate; used of the Gadarene whom no man could bind, and of the tongue which no man can tame)
Old English tam, domesticated. The Greek damazo means to subdue or break in, used of animals and of men — and in James of the one member of the body that resists it.

Biblical Definition

Mark uses the word of the man among the tombs: “Because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces: neither could any man tame him” (Mark 5:4). Every restraint had been tried and had failed — and the Lord delivered him with a word, and he was found sitting, clothed, and in his right mind. James applies the same verb to something nearer home: “For every kind of beasts, and of birds, and of serpents, and of things in the sea, is tamed, and hath been tamed of mankind: But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison” (James 3:7-8). The argument moves from the greater to the lesser and lands on an absurdity: man has subdued every order of creature and cannot govern one small member of his own body. James has already said why: “the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity… and it is set on fire of hell” (James 3:6). And he names the specific inconsistency: “Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God” (James 3:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines tame as having lost its native wildness and shyness, domestic, and to tame as to reclaim or subdue.

expand to see more

TAME, a. Having lost its native wildness and shyness; domestic; gentle.

2. Crushed; subdued; depressed; spiritless.

TAME, v.t. To reclaim; to reduce from a wild to a domestic state; to make gentle and familiar.

2. To subdue; to conquer; to depress; as, to tame the pride of men.

UNRULY, a. Disregarding restraint; licentious; disposed to violate laws; turbulent; ungovernable.

Key Scripture

James 3:8 — "But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison."

James 3:7 — "For every kind of beasts, and of birds, and of serpents, and of things in the sea, is tamed, and hath been tamed of mankind:"

James 3:9 — "Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God."

Mark 5:4 — "Because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces: neither could any man tame him."

Modern Corruption

Sins of speech are ranked as minor, and James makes the tongue the test of whether a man's religion is real at all.

expand to see more

James has already said that a man who seems to be religious and bridleth not his tongue deceives his own heart, and that his religion is vain. That is an extraordinary weight to place on speech, and it is out of all proportion to how the matter is usually treated. Gossip, slander, contempt, the cutting remark, the anonymous comment — these are the ordinary sins of respectable congregations, and they are rarely disciplined and seldom confessed. James calls the tongue a fire, a world of iniquity, set on fire of hell. A church that would remove a man for drunkenness and tolerate a lifetime of destructive speech has not weighed the epistle it reads.

The two texts together supply the answer to the despair James's words might otherwise produce. No man can tame the tongue — and neither could any man tame the Gadarene, until One came who was not merely a man. The chains had all failed and the Lord spoke and the man sat clothed and in his right mind. James is not saying the tongue cannot be governed; he is saying no man can do it, which drives the reader to the only One who can. The remedy is not a technique of self-control but the same power that emptied a legion out of a man among the tombs, and it works on the heart, since out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek damazo (G1150), to tame or subdue — Mark 5:4, James 3:7-8; akatascheton (G183), unruly — James 3:8; chalinagogeo (G5468), to bridle — James 1:26.

expand to see more

Greek damazo (G1150) — to subdue, tame; Mark 5:4 of the Gadarene, and James 3:7-8 of beasts and of the tongue.

Greek akatascheton (G183) — that cannot be restrained; James 3:8, its only occurrence.

Greek chalinagogeo (G5468) — to lead with a bridle; James 1:26 and 3:2, the figure James prefers for speech.

Greek homoiosis (G3669) — similitude, likeness; James 3:9, men made after the similitude of God — the reason cursing them is monstrous.

Matthew 12:34 locates the root: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.

Usage

"“The tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil” — and no man could tame the Gadarene either."

"“Therewith bless we God… and therewith curse we men” — the same mouth."

"Every order of creature subdued, and one small member ungoverned."
